title: The Big Picture
tagline: How Claude Code's extensibility layers fit together — and which to reach for.
whatItIs: Claude Code is not just a chat box — it's an agentic harness you can extend at six layers. Each layer answers a different question:
mentalModel: Think of Claude as a new senior engineer. Instructions are their onboarding doc, Skills are playbooks they pull off the shelf, Subagents are teammates they delegate to, Hooks are the CI/policy gates they can't bypass, MCP is their access to your internal systems, and Plugins are how you ship all of that to the whole company at once.
whenToUse: Instructions (CLAUDE.md) → "Always know this about my project." Persistent context & rules.
Skills → "When this kind of task comes up, follow this procedure." Reusable, model-invoked know-how.
Subagents → "Delegate this to a focused specialist with its own context window."
Hooks → "This must happen automatically / this must never happen." Deterministic, not the model's choice.
MCP → "Give Claude a new sense or limb" — access to a DB, API, ticketing system, or internal service.
Plugins → "Package all of the above and distribute it across the org."

anatomy.location: Project-level config lives in .claude/ at your repo root; personal config in ~/.claude/. Settings & hooks in settings.json; MCP in .mcp.json.
anatomy.format: Markdown + frontmatter for content; JSON for config.

steps: Read the map. Each following lesson is one layer, in the order you should learn them.
Do the lab in each. The lessons are practical — you'll actually create a file or config each time.
Copy from examples/. Every lesson has a matching real file in ai-features-lab/examples/ you can drop into a project.
Finish with the Capstone — you'll assemble one feature of each layer into an enterprise 'golden setup'.

code.file: Mental model — one repo, all six layers
code.body:
your-enterprise-repo/
├── CLAUDE.md                      # 1. Instructions  (always-on project memory)
├── .mcp.json                      # 5. MCP servers   (DB, Jira, internal APIs)
├── .claude/
│   ├── settings.json              # 4. Hooks         (policy gates, auto-format)
│   ├── skills/
│   │   └── pr-summary/SKILL.md    # 2. Skills        (reusable procedures)
│   ├── agents/
│   │   └── security-auditor.md    # 3. Subagents     (focused specialists)
│   └── commands/
│       └── release-notes.md       #    Slash commands (typed shortcuts)
└── (plugins distribute all of the above to every developer) # 6. Plugins

enterprise: Standardize how 200 engineers use AI: ship one plugin, everyone gets the same guardrails.
Encode compliance as hooks so risky commands are blocked deterministically, not 'usually'.
Connect Claude to your internal systems (Jira, Snowflake, Confluence) via MCP — without leaking credentials into prompts.

lab.goal: Get oriented in a real repo before you build anything.
steps: Open a terminal in any project and run ls -a. Look for a .claude/ folder or CLAUDE.md.
In Claude Code, type /help and then /agents, /mcp, and /plugin to see what's already configured.
Predict which of the six layers would best solve a pain point you have today. Keep it in mind — you'll build it by the end.

pitfalls: Don't cram everything into CLAUDE.md — it's always in context and costs tokens on every turn.
Don't reach for a hook when a skill will do, or a skill when a one-line instruction will do. Use the lightest layer that works.

quiz.q: You want a destructive shell command (like a prod DB drop) to be impossible for Claude to run — not just discouraged. Which layer?
quiz.explain: Instructions are guidance the model *usually* follows. A PreToolUse hook is run by the harness and can BLOCK the tool call with exit code 2 — that's deterministic enforcement, which is what 'impossible, not discouraged' requires.

title: Instructions & Memory
tagline: CLAUDE.md — the always-on briefing that shapes every response.
whatItIs: Instructions are persistent context Claude Code loads automatically at the start of a session. The primary mechanism is the CLAUDE.md memory file. It's where project conventions, commands, architecture notes, and 'golden rules' live so you never have to re-explain them.
mentalModel: CLAUDE.md is the onboarding wiki you hand a new hire on day one — except the model re-reads it every single time it works.
whenToUse: Project-wide facts: stack, build/test commands, folder map, conventions.
Non-negotiable rules: 'never commit to main', 'all code needs tests'.
Gotchas a newcomer would trip over: frozen folders, one-way migrations.
NOT for one-off task details (just say those in chat) or huge reference docs (link or import them instead).

anatomy.location: ./CLAUDE.md (project, committed & shared) · ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (personal, all projects) · ./CLAUDE.local.md (personal, this project, gitignored) · nested CLAUDE.md in subfolders (loaded when work touches them).
anatomy.format: Plain Markdown. Use @path/to/file to import another file's contents. Keep it tight — it's in context on every turn.

steps: Create the file. At your repo root, run claude then type /init — Claude scans the repo and drafts a CLAUDE.md for you. Or create it by hand.
Lead with the golden rules. The things that must never be violated go near the top.
List the commands. Install / test / lint / run — so Claude verifies its own work the way you do.
Add a codebase map. A few lines on where things live saves dozens of search turns.
Add a quick memory on the fly. In a session, start a line with # and Claude offers to save it to memory.
Keep it lean. Re-read it monthly; delete anything stale. Every line costs tokens on every request.

code.body:
# CLAUDE.md — project memory & instructions

## Golden rules
- Never commit directly to `main`. Branch, then open a PR.
- All new code needs tests; run `npm test` before calling a change done.
- Secrets live in `.env` (gitignored) — never hardcode them.

## Commands
- Install: `npm ci`
- Test:    `npm test`   (single: `npm test -- path/to/test`)
- Lint:    `npm run lint`

## Codebase map
- `src/api/`    HTTP handlers
- `src/domain/` business logic (no I/O)
- `src/db/`     data access

## Things that will bite you
- `legacy/` is frozen — do not modify.
- Migrations are one-way; never edit a committed one, add a new one.

<!-- Import shared standards instead of pasting them: -->
@docs/engineering-standards.md

enterprise: A root CLAUDE.md committed to the repo gives every engineer (and every AI session) the same source of truth — onboarding drops from days to minutes.
Nested CLAUDE.md files let a monorepo give service-specific rules only when work touches that service.
Personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md carries your cross-project preferences (commit style, language) without polluting team repos.

lab.goal: Give a real project a memory.
steps: Open Claude Code in a project and run /init (or copy examples/instructions/CLAUDE.md and edit it).
Add three golden rules that are actually true for your project.
Start a new line in chat with # and type a fact like 'we deploy on Fridays' — accept the save and watch it land in CLAUDE.md.
Ask Claude 'how do I run the tests here?' — it should answer from your file without searching.

pitfalls: Bloat: a 600-line CLAUDE.md silently taxes every request. Be ruthless.
Stale rules are worse than none — they actively mislead. Treat it like code: review it.
Don't put secrets in CLAUDE.md; it's committed and goes into context.

quiz.q: Where do you put a rule that should apply to YOU across every repo, but not be forced on teammates?
quiz.explain: User-level memory at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies to all your projects and isn't committed, so it stays personal. The project CLAUDE.md is shared with the team via git.

title: Skills
tagline: Reusable procedures Claude pulls off the shelf when the task fits.
whatItIs: A Skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file: a named, described procedure Claude loads on demand when a task matches its description. Skills can also bundle scripts and reference files. The magic is progressive disclosure — only the short description sits in context until the skill is actually needed, then the full instructions load.
mentalModel: A skill is a playbook in a binder. Claude reads the spine labels (the descriptions) cheaply, and only opens the binder it needs for the task at hand.
whenToUse: A repeatable task with a 'right way' to do it: writing PR descriptions, generating migrations, formatting an incident report.
Procedures that bundle helper scripts or templates the model should use.
Knowledge too big or too situational for always-on CLAUDE.md.
NOT for a single fact (use instructions) or for spawning a separate context (use a subagent).

anatomy.location: .claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md (project) or ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (personal). Plugins can ship skills too.
anatomy.format: Markdown with YAML frontmatter requiring name and description. The folder may also contain scripts, templates, and resource files the skill references.

steps: Make the folder: .claude/skills/pr-summary/.
Write SKILL.md frontmatter. name (kebab-case) and a description that says what it does AND when to use it — this is what Claude matches against, so be specific.
Write the body as clear, numbered instructions. Include an output template and guardrails.
(Optional) Add resources in the same folder — a template.md, a validate.py — and reference them by relative path from SKILL.md.
Invoke it. Claude triggers it automatically when a task matches, or you can type /pr-summary to run it explicitly.
Iterate the description. If it triggers too often or not enough, tune the description first — that's the dial.

code.body:
---
name: pr-summary
description: Generate a structured PR description from the current git diff.
  Use when the user asks to summarize changes, write a PR description, or
  prep release notes for a branch.
---

# PR Summary Skill

## Steps
1. Run `git diff --stat` and `git diff` to gather the change set.
2. Group changes: feature / fix / refactor / tests / docs.
3. Fill the template below — describe what changed, factually.

## Output template
\`\`\`
## What changed
<one paragraph>

## Changes by area
- **Feature:** ...
- **Fix:** ...

## How to verify
1. ...
\`\`\`

## Guardrails
- Never invent a ticket number — write "TODO: link ticket" if absent.
- Flag auth/billing/migration changes under "⚠️ Needs careful review".

enterprise: Codify your org's PR, incident, and ADR (architecture decision record) formats as skills — every output is consistent regardless of who's driving.
Ship domain procedures: 'how we write a Terraform module', 'how we add a feature flag', bundled with validation scripts.
Distribute skills org-wide inside a plugin so a new team inherits institutional know-how on day one.

lab.goal: Build and trigger your first skill.
steps: Copy examples/skills/pr-summary/SKILL.md into .claude/skills/pr-summary/SKILL.md in a git repo.
Make a trivial change to any file (don't commit).
In Claude Code, type /pr-summary — confirm it reads your diff and produces the templated output.
Now tighten the description to also trigger on the phrase 'describe my branch', and verify Claude picks it up automatically when you ask that.

pitfalls: Vague descriptions are the #1 failure — 'helps with PRs' won't match reliably. Say exactly when to use it.
Don't dump a novel in SKILL.md; keep the always-loaded part lean and push detail into referenced files.
A skill is instructions, not a sandbox — it runs in your main session's context and permissions.

quiz.q: Why does the 'description' field matter more than almost anything else in a skill?
options: It's shown in the UI only
It's what Claude matches against to decide when to load the skill
quiz.explain: Thanks to progressive disclosure, only the name+description stay in context. Claude uses the description to decide whether the task fits, so a precise 'what + when' is what makes a skill fire at the right time.

title: Subagents
tagline: Delegate to a focused specialist with its own context window and tools.
whatItIs: A subagent is a separate Claude instance your main session can delegate a task to. It has its own context window, its own system prompt, and a restricted toolset. The main agent hands off a task, the subagent works in isolation, and only its final result comes back — keeping your main context clean.
mentalModel: Subagents are teammates you assign a ticket to. They go off, do the work in their own headspace, and report back a summary — you don't absorb every file they read.
whenToUse: Focused, well-scoped jobs: 'audit this for security', 'find everywhere X is used', 'write tests for this module'.
Work that would flood your main context with noise (large searches, log triage).
Tasks needing a different 'persona' or a restricted toolset (e.g. read-only reviewer).
NOT for tiny tasks (delegation has overhead) or work needing tight back-and-forth with you.

anatomy.format: Markdown system prompt with YAML frontmatter: name, description (when to delegate — say 'use PROACTIVELY' to encourage auto-use), optional tools (allowlist; omit to inherit all), optional model.

steps: Run /agents and choose 'Create new agent' — or hand-write the file.
Name + describe. The description tells the main agent when to delegate. Add 'use PROACTIVELY' for jobs that should auto-trigger.
Restrict tools in frontmatter. A reviewer should get Read, Grep, Glob, Bash — no Write. Least privilege matters.
Pick a model if you want — a cheap model for triage, a strong one for deep review.
Write the system prompt as the body: role, scope, what to look for, and an exact output format.
Invoke: ask the main agent to delegate, or say 'use the security-auditor subagent on this diff'.

code.body:
---
name: security-auditor
description: Read-only security reviewer for a code change. Use PROACTIVELY
  before merging anything touching auth, input handling, or secrets.
  Returns a prioritized findings list — it does not edit code.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: sonnet
---

You are a senior application-security engineer reviewing a code change.

## Scope
- Review only the diff/files you're pointed at. Never refactor.
- Read-only tools only; use Bash for SAST (semgrep, npm audit), not edits.

## Look for (priority order)
1. Injection (SQL/command/template, unsafe eval)
2. Broken authN/authZ, privilege escalation
3. Hardcoded secrets / secrets in logs
4. Unvalidated input reaching a sink; SSRF

## Output
Per finding: Severity · file:line · Issue · Why it matters · Fix.
End with: "SAFE TO MERGE" or "BLOCK — N critical/high findings".

enterprise: A read-only security-auditor and pii-scanner that run before merges — guardrails that scale across teams.
A cheap-model triage agent fans out across logs/tickets, escalating only what matters to a strong-model agent.
Domain specialists: a db-migration agent, a terraform-reviewer agent — each with exactly the tools it needs and nothing more (least privilege).

lab.goal: Delegate a real review to a specialist.
steps: Copy examples/agents/security-auditor.md into .claude/agents/.
Run /agents and confirm it appears in the list.
Make a small code change with an obvious issue (e.g. a hardcoded API key) in a scratch file.
Ask Claude: 'Use the security-auditor subagent to review my changes.' Confirm it returns findings and a verdict — and that your main context stays clean.

pitfalls: Giving a reviewer Write/Edit tools defeats the point — restrict the toolset.
Over-delegation adds latency and token cost; only delegate work that's genuinely separable.
The subagent can't see your main conversation — give it everything it needs in the delegation prompt.

quiz.q: What's the main reason to send a large codebase search to a subagent instead of doing it inline?
options: It keeps the noisy intermediate results out of your main context window
Subagents can edit files the main agent can't
It's the only way to use Grep
quiz.explain: A subagent works in its own context window and returns only a final summary. That isolation keeps hundreds of file-read lines out of your main session, preserving its context budget.

title: Hooks
tagline: Deterministic automation the harness runs — not the model's choice.
whatItIs: Hooks are shell commands the Claude Code harness runs automatically at defined lifecycle events. Unlike instructions (which the model may or may not follow), hooks always fire. They can observe, inject context, or block an action. This is how you turn 'please don't' into 'cannot'.
mentalModel: Hooks are the CI pipeline and the office keycard reader of your AI session: deterministic gates that run regardless of what the model 'decides'.
whenToUse: Enforce policy: block dangerous Bash commands, prevent edits to protected paths.
Auto-format / auto-lint every file Claude writes (PostToolUse).
Inject always-on context at prompt time (UserPromptSubmit stdout is added to context).
Audit & telemetry: log every session or tool use centrally (Stop / PostToolUse).
NOT for judgment calls that need the model's reasoning — that's a skill or subagent.

anatomy.format: JSON. Events include PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop, SessionStart, Notification, PreCompact. Each has a matcher (e.g. tool name) and a list of command hooks.

steps: Pick the event. Want to stop something before it runs? PreToolUse. React after? PostToolUse. Add context to every prompt? UserPromptSubmit.
Set the matcher. e.g. "Bash" to target shell calls, or "Edit|Write" for file writes.
Write the command. It receives a JSON payload on stdin (tool name, inputs, file paths). Read it in your script.
Control flow with exit codes. In a PreToolUse hook, exit 2 BLOCKS the action and sends your stderr back to Claude; exit 0 allows. stdout from UserPromptSubmit is injected into context.
Use env vars like $CLAUDE_FILE_PATHS for convenience in simple one-liners.
Test it by triggering the matching action and watching it fire (or block).
enterprise: Compliance as code: a PreToolUse Bash guard makes prod-destructive commands literally un-runnable by Claude — auditable and uniform.
Zero-style-debate: PostToolUse Prettier/ESLint means AI-written code always matches house style before review.
Traceability: a Stop hook appends a signed record of each AI session to a central log for SOC2 / audit.
Always-on guardrails: UserPromptSubmit injects current policy reminders into every single turn.

lab.goal: Block a dangerous command and auto-format a write.
steps: Copy examples/hooks/guard-bash.js to .claude/hooks/guard-bash.js and the hooks block from examples/hooks/settings.hooks.json into .claude/settings.json.
Restart Claude Code so it loads the settings.
Ask Claude to run rm -rf /tmp/whatever (harmless target but matches the pattern variant) — actually test with git push --force on a throwaway branch. Confirm it's blocked with your message.
Ask Claude to create a messy-formatted JS file and confirm the PostToolUse Prettier hook cleans it automatically.

pitfalls: Hooks run with YOUR shell privileges — a buggy hook can do real damage. Review hook code like production code.
Only exit code 2 blocks in PreToolUse; other non-zero codes surface an error but may not block. Read the payload, be precise.
Slow hooks slow every matching action. Keep them fast; fail open where safety allows.
Hooks are powerful and run automatically — never install hooks from an untrusted source without reading them.

quiz.q: In a PreToolUse hook, what does exiting with code 2 do?
options: Logs a warning but lets the tool run
Blocks the tool call and feeds your stderr back to Claude
quiz.explain: Exit code 2 from a PreToolUse hook blocks the tool call. Whatever you print to stderr is returned to Claude as the reason, so it can adapt. Exit 0 allows the call.

title: MCP Servers
tagline: Model Context Protocol — give Claude access to your real systems.
whatItIs: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting Claude to external tools and data. An MCP server exposes tools (actions), resources (data), and prompts over a standard interface. Add a Postgres server and Claude can query your DB; add a Jira server and it can read/file tickets — all without you pasting data or secrets into the chat.
mentalModel: MCP is USB-C for AI. The server is the device (a DB, an API, a filesystem); the protocol is the universal port. Plug it in and Claude gains a new capability.
whenToUse: Claude needs live data from a system: database, data warehouse, ticketing, monitoring, docs.
You want a capability reused across many tools/clients via one standard server.
Sensitive access where you want auth handled by the server, not embedded in prompts.
NOT when a simple Bash command or local file read already does the job — don't over-engineer.

anatomy.location: Project: .mcp.json at repo root (shared via git). User/local scope via the CLI: claude mcp add. Inspect with /mcp.
anatomy.format: JSON under mcpServers. Transports: stdio (Claude launches a local command), and http/sse (a remote url). Pass secrets via ${ENV_VARS}, never inline.

steps: Find or build a server. Many exist (@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres, -filesystem, GitHub, etc.); or build one with the MCP SDK.
Add it. Quick way: claude mcp add postgres -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres. Team way: commit a .mcp.json.
Wire secrets via env. Reference ${DATABASE_URL}; keep the real value in your environment, not the file.
Choose the transport. Local tool → stdio. Internal/remote service → http/sse with an Authorization header from an env var.
Verify with /mcp — it lists servers, their tools, and connection status.
Use it. Ask Claude something only the server can answer ('how many users signed up yesterday?') and it'll call the server's tools.
enterprise: Read-only warehouse access (Snowflake/Postgres) lets Claude answer data questions and draft analyses — with permissions enforced by the server.
Internal bridges: a Jira/Confluence/ServiceNow MCP server turns Claude into a teammate that reads tickets and drafts docs against real context.
Govern it: distribute approved MCP servers via a plugin, and combine with hooks to log every MCP tool call for audit.
Security posture: secrets stay in the server's environment and IAM; they never enter the model's prompt or transcript.

lab.goal: Connect Claude to a local filesystem MCP server (zero credentials needed).
steps: Create a ./docs folder with a couple of markdown files.
Run claude mcp add fs -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem ./docs (or copy the filesystem-docs entry from examples/mcp/.mcp.json).
Run /mcp and confirm the server is connected and lists its tools.
Ask Claude: 'Using the fs MCP server, summarize what's in my docs folder.' Confirm it calls the server rather than guessing.

pitfalls: Never inline secrets in .mcp.json — it's committed. Always use ${ENV} indirection.
MCP servers run code and may have broad access; only add servers you trust, and prefer read-only scopes.
Too many servers/tools bloat the tool list and confuse selection. Add what you need.
A committed .mcp.json shares the server config but not the secrets — teammates still set their own env vars.

quiz.q: Your .mcp.json is committed to git. How should the database password reach the Postgres MCP server?
options: Via a ${ENV_VAR} reference resolved from the environment
Pasted into the chat each session
quiz.explain: Use ${ENV_VAR} indirection so the committed file only references the secret. The actual value lives in each developer's environment / a secrets manager — never in the repo or the prompt.

title: Slash Commands
tagline: Typed shortcuts that expand into a prompt — your team's macros.
whatItIs: A slash command is a Markdown file that becomes a typed shortcut like /release-notes. It expands into a prompt template you control, can take $ARGUMENTS, and can even embed live shell output with !`cmd`. Think of it as a saved, parameterized prompt the whole team can run.
mentalModel: Slash commands are keyboard macros for prompts. Skills are model-invoked playbooks; slash commands are human-invoked ones you type on demand.
whenToUse: A prompt you run often and want to standardize: '/release-notes', '/triage', '/explain-this'.
Workflows that should pull in fresh context (git log, test output) at run time.
Lightweight team tooling that doesn't need a whole skill folder.

anatomy.format: Markdown body = the prompt. Optional frontmatter: description, argument-hint, allowed-tools. Use $ARGUMENTS for input and !`shell` to inline command output.

steps: Create the file: .claude/commands/release-notes.md → becomes /release-notes.
Write the prompt body describing exactly what you want done.
Add dynamic context with !`git log ...` — it runs when the command is invoked and inlines the output.
Accept input with $ARGUMENTS (and document it via argument-hint).
Scope tools with allowed-tools so the command can only do what it needs.
Type /release-notes v1.2.0 to run it.

code.body:
---
description: Draft release notes from commits since the last tag.
argument-hint: "[since-tag]"
allowed-tools: Bash(git*), Read
---

Generate customer-facing release notes.

- Last tag: !\`git describe --tags --abbrev=0\`
- Commits:  !\`git log $(git describe --tags --abbrev=0)..HEAD --pretty=%s\`

Arguments: $ARGUMENTS

Task:
1. Group commits into Features / Fixes / Internal.
2. Rewrite each in plain user-benefit language.
3. Output markdown with a version heading and today's date.

enterprise: Standardize recurring workflows (release notes, incident triage, onboarding walkthroughs) as one-word commands.
Embed live context so commands are always current — no stale copy-paste prompts in a wiki.
Ship them in a plugin so every repo gets the same command palette.

lab.goal: Create a working slash command with live git context.
steps: Copy examples/commands/release-notes.md into .claude/commands/.
In a repo with a few commits, type /release-notes.
Confirm the !`git log` output is inlined and the notes are grouped & rewritten.
Add a $ARGUMENTS use (e.g. a target audience) and run /release-notes executives.

pitfalls: Commands you type vs. skills the model auto-picks — choose based on who decides to run it.
!`shell` runs every invocation; keep it fast and side-effect-free.
Scope allowed-tools — a command that only reads git shouldn't be able to Write.

quiz.q: What's the key difference between a slash command and a skill?
options: Slash commands are invoked by the human typing them; skills are auto-selected by the model when a task matches
Slash commands run on a server
quiz.explain: A slash command is a human-typed shortcut. A skill is model-invoked: Claude reads skill descriptions and loads one when the task fits. Same spirit (reusable prompts/procedures), different trigger.

title: Plugins & Marketplaces
tagline: Bundle everything above and distribute it across the whole org.
whatItIs: A plugin is a folder that bundles any combination of commands, skills, subagents, hooks, and MCP servers behind a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest. A marketplace is a git repo that lists plugins. Together they let a platform team ship one install that gives every developer the same skills, agents, guardrails, and integrations.
mentalModel: If the other five layers are apps, a plugin is the signed installer and the marketplace is your company's internal app store.
whenToUse: You've built useful skills/agents/hooks/MCP and want to share them beyond one repo.
You need consistency and governance across many teams.
You want versioned, updatable distribution (bump version → everyone updates).
NOT for a one-off personal tweak — just keep that in your ~/.claude/.

anatomy.location: A plugin folder with .claude-plugin/plugin.json. A marketplace is a repo with a .claude-plugin/marketplace.json listing plugins. Installed via the /plugin command.
anatomy.format: plugin.json declares name, version, and paths to the commands/agents/skills/hooks/mcpServers it ships.

steps: Lay out the folder. Put your commands/, skills/, agents/, hooks/, and .mcp.json inside one plugin directory.
Write the manifest: .claude-plugin/plugin.json with name, version, and the paths to each bundled part.
Publish a marketplace. Create a git repo with .claude-plugin/marketplace.json that lists your plugin(s) and where they live.
Add the marketplace: users run /plugin marketplace add your-org/claude-marketplace.
Install: /plugin install enterprise-toolkit — the user instantly gets all bundled features.
Ship updates by bumping version and re-publishing; users update from the /plugin menu.

code.body:
{
  "name": "enterprise-toolkit",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Company-standard bundle: review skills, a security-auditor
    agent, policy hooks, and the internal knowledge-base MCP server.",
  "author": { "name": "Platform Engineering", "email": "platform@example.com" },
  "commands": "./commands",
  "agents": "./agents",
  "skills": "./skills",
  "hooks": "./hooks/hooks.json",
  "mcpServers": "./.mcp.json"
}

enterprise: One install = the org's entire AI guardrail stack: review skills + security agent + policy hooks + approved MCP servers.
Governance & versioning: roll out a new compliance hook to 500 engineers by publishing v1.1.0.
Per-team marketplaces: the data team ships warehouse MCP + query skills; the platform team ships infra agents — devs install what they need.
Onboarding: a new hire runs two /plugin commands and inherits years of institutional tooling.

lab.goal: Package your skill + agent + hook into one plugin.
steps: Use the scaffold in examples/plugins/enterprise-toolkit/. Drop your pr-summary skill, security-auditor agent, and a hooks/hooks.json inside it.
Confirm .claude-plugin/plugin.json points at each folder.
Create a local marketplace repo with a marketplace.json listing the plugin (see the code samples above).
Run /plugin marketplace add <path-or-repo> then /plugin install enterprise-toolkit, and verify the skill, agent, and hook all show up.

pitfalls: Version discipline matters — consumers update based on the version field; bump it on every change.
A plugin can ship hooks and MCP servers that run code: publish only from trusted, reviewed sources, and have consumers read what they install.
Keep plugins focused; a mega-plugin that ships everything is hard to reason about and govern.

quiz.q: Your platform team wants 300 engineers to all get the same security agent and policy hooks, with easy updates. Best approach?
options: Email everyone a zip of .claude files
Publish a plugin to an internal marketplace and have devs /plugin install it
Put it all in each repo's CLAUDE.md
Ask each team to rebuild it
quiz.explain: Plugins + a marketplace give versioned, one-command distribution and updates. Bundling skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers into one installable package is exactly the enterprise standardization use case.

title: Case Study: SafePay
tagline: A real payments-platform problem, solved end-to-end with all six layers.
whatItIs: SafePay is a 200-engineer payments platform (think Stripe-lite). Leadership wants to adopt Claude Code to move faster — but payments means real money, PII, and auditors. This lesson walks the actual pains and shows which layer removes each one. The point isn't 'look what features exist' — it's start from the problem, pick the lightest layer that solves it.
mentalModel: Don't ask 'what can this feature do?' Ask 'what hurts, and which layer makes that pain impossible?' Match symptoms to layers.
whenToUse: Symptom: new hires take 3 weeks to ramp → encode the project in Instructions (CLAUDE.md).
Symptom: every PR / incident report looks different → standardize with Skills.
Symptom: security review is a merge bottleneck → a read-only security-auditor subagent pre-screens.
Symptom: fear that AI could drop a prod table or commit a secret → make it impossible with Hooks.
Symptom: engineers tab between Jira, Postgres, Confluence all day → connect them via MCP.
Symptom: 200 engineers, no two setups alike → ship one Plugin from an internal marketplace.

anatomy.location: The pain inventory → solution map. Each problem gets the lightest layer that fully solves it — guidance for judgment, enforcement only for safety-critical rules.
anatomy.format: Phased rollout: ship instructions+skills first (low risk, fast win), then subagents+MCP (capability), then hooks+plugin (governance & scale).

steps: Phase 1 — Win trust (week 1). Add a tight CLAUDE.md (golden rules, commands, architecture map) and the pr-summary + incident-report skills. Engineers feel faster immediately; zero risk.
Phase 2 — Add capability (week 2–3). Add the read-only security-auditor and test-writer subagents, and wire read-only MCP to Postgres, Jira, and Confluence so Claude answers from real data.
Phase 3 — Add governance (week 4). Turn on hooks: guard-bash blocks prod-destructive commands, a PII-scan PostToolUse hook, and a Stop audit-log for SOC2.
Phase 4 — Scale it (week 5). Bundle all of the above into the safepay-toolkit plugin and publish to the internal marketplace. Every engineer runs two /plugin commands and inherits the whole setup.
Phase 5 — Iterate. Track metrics, tune skill descriptions, version the plugin. Roll a new compliance hook to all 200 engineers by bumping a version.

code.body:
PROBLEM                              LAYER (solution)             ENFORCED?   OUTCOME
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Slow onboarding, tribal knowledge    Instructions (CLAUDE.md)     guided      ramp 3wk -> 3d
Inconsistent PRs / incident docs     Skills (pr-summary, etc.)    guided      uniform output
Security review bottleneck           Subagent (security-auditor)  guided      pre-screened PRs
Flaky / missing tests                Subagent (test-writer)       guided      coverage up
"AI might drop a prod table"         Hook (guard-bash, exit 2)    ENFORCED    cannot happen
"AI might commit a secret/PII"       Hook (PostToolUse pii-scan)  ENFORCED    blocked + logged
Auditors need a trail                Hook (Stop -> audit.log)     ENFORCED    SOC2 evidence
Context-hunting across systems       MCP (Postgres/Jira/Confl.)   capability  answers from data
200 engineers, no two setups alike   Plugin + marketplace         scale       one-command install

RULE OF THUMB:
  - Judgment / formatting / knowledge  -> guide it (instructions, skills, subagents)
  - Safety-critical, must-never-happen -> enforce it (hooks)
  - Access to real systems             -> connect it (MCP)
  - Consistency across the org         -> distribute it (plugin)

enterprise: Outcome — onboarding: a committed CLAUDE.md + skills cut effective ramp time from weeks to days.
Outcome — safety: destructive prod commands are deterministically blocked, not 'usually avoided' — the difference an auditor cares about.
Outcome — throughput: the security-auditor subagent clears trivial reviews so humans focus on the 10% that need judgment.
Outcome — compliance: every AI session is logged centrally; secret/PII writes are blocked at the hook layer.
Outcome — consistency: one versioned plugin means all 200 engineers share identical guardrails, updated centrally.

lab.goal: Build one vertical slice of the SafePay setup.
steps: Pick ONE pain from the table above that you actually have at work.
Implement the matching layer using the relevant examples/ file (e.g. the guard-bash hook for 'AI might drop a prod table').
Write 2–3 sentences: what was the pain, which layer, and is it enforced or guided — and why that's the right call.
Bonus: sketch how you'd phase the full rollout to YOUR team in 5 weeks, mirroring the phases above.

pitfalls: Leading with hooks (enforcement) before delivering value (skills) makes the tool feel like a cop. Win trust first, govern second.
Enforcing judgment calls ('PRs must be phrased like X' as a hard block) backfires — guide those, enforce only safety.
Skipping the metrics step means you can't show ROI and the rollout stalls at one team.

quiz.q: SafePay's auditors require proof that a prod database drop is *impossible* via Claude, not just discouraged. Which layer, and why?
options: Instructions — write 'never drop prod' in CLAUDE.md
A Skill that explains safe DB practices
A PreToolUse Hook that exits 2 on matching commands — deterministic, harness-enforced
quiz.explain: Auditors need deterministic enforcement. Instructions and skills are guidance the model usually follows. Only a hook is run by the harness and can hard-block the command (exit 2) and log it — that's defensible evidence.

title: Real-World Build Projects
tagline: Production-grade dev tools you can actually build and ship with these features.
whatItIs: These aren't toy katas — they're real engineering projects a team would put on a roadmap. Each one is a piece of developer software (a bot, a service, a CLI, a plugin) built on the Claude API and/or Claude Code's feature layers. Every card gives the problem, tech stack, the AI features it uses, and concrete deliverables so you can scope it like a real ticket.
mentalModel: Think product, not exercise: each project is something you could demo to your team on Friday and merge to a real repo.
whenToUse: When you want a portfolio piece that proves you can ship AI-powered dev tooling.
When a real pain on your team maps to one of these — build it for keeps.
As the seed for the Capstone: the platform-grade builds become your org's golden setup.

anatomy.location: Build each in its own repo with a proper stack (CI, tests, README). Wire Claude Code's feature layers into the dev workflow, and use the Claude API (@anthropic-ai/sdk) where the tool runs as a service.
anatomy.format: Each card: Problem → Stack → AI features → Deliverables. 🟢 weekend build · 🟡 a sprint · 🔴 a real internal product.

steps: Pick a project whose problem you actually have.
Scaffold a real repo — package manager, CI, tests, README. Treat it like production code.
Wire the AI features listed on the card (Claude Code layers for the dev workflow; the Claude API for runtime services).
Ship a thin vertical slice first, then iterate to the full deliverables.
Add guardrails — hooks/tests/CI — before you call it done. AI tooling needs the same rigor as any service.

projects.title: AI commit & PR assistant (Git hook + CLI)
projects.problem: Commit messages and PR descriptions are inconsistent and low-context.
acceptance: CLI reads the staged diff and drafts a Conventional-Commits message
`/pr-summary` skill produces a templated PR body from the branch diff
Packaged as an installable npm bin + a prepare-commit-msg git hook

projects.title: Repo onboarding bot
projects.problem: New engineers lose days finding how to build, test, and navigate a repo.
acceptance: A generated CLAUDE.md (golden rules, commands, folder map) committed to the repo
An `/onboard` skill that walks a newcomer through first build + first test
Answers 'how do I run X?' with zero repo searching

projects.title: AI code-review GitHub Action
projects.problem: Review is a bottleneck; trivial issues slip through and reviewers burn out.
acceptance: On every PR, posts inline review comments grouped by severity
A security-focused pass flags injection / authz / secret issues
Caches the repo context to keep cost per PR low; fails the check only on criticals

projects.title: Internal docs copilot (RAG over MCP)
projects.problem: Tribal knowledge is scattered across Confluence, READMEs, and runbooks.
acceptance: A custom MCP server exposes a `search_docs` tool backed by a vector index
Claude answers questions by citing the actual source doc + section
Index refresh job keeps answers current; secrets via ${ENV}, never inline

projects.title: Test-generation service + CI gate
projects.problem: Coverage is low and writing tests is tedious, so it never happens.
acceptance: A test-writer subagent generates tests for a target module that actually run + pass
CI step proposes tests for files whose coverage dropped in the PR
Generated code is auto-formatted and linted before commit

projects.title: Incident-response companion (Slack bot)
projects.problem: During incidents, responders manually grep logs, dashboards, and runbooks under pressure.
acceptance: Bot summarizes an alert, pulls recent logs/metrics via MCP, and proposes next steps
Drafts a timeline + postmortem skeleton from the channel history
Every AI action is written to a tamper-evident audit log for the review

projects.title: Self-serve data Q&A assistant
projects.problem: Analysts and support manually query the warehouse for routine questions.
acceptance: Read-only MCP connection with credentials via ${ENV}; row/cost limits enforced
Natural-language questions return correct results + the SQL used (for trust)
A guard hook blocks any non-SELECT statement

projects.title: Org-wide compliance & tooling plugin
projects.problem: Every team hand-rolls its own .claude config; guardrails are inconsistent.
acceptance: One plugin bundles review skills, a security agent, policy hooks, and approved MCP servers
Published to an internal marketplace; installable in two `/plugin` commands
Versioned — a new compliance hook rolls out by bumping the version

code.body:
MILESTONE 1  🟢  Repo onboarding bot           (Instructions + Skill)
             🟢  AI commit & PR assistant       (Skill + CLI + Claude API)

MILESTONE 2  🟡  AI code-review GitHub Action    (Subagent pattern + API)
             🟡  Test-generation service + CI    (Subagent + Hook)
             🟡  Internal docs copilot (RAG)     (custom MCP server)

MILESTONE 3  🔴  Self-serve data Q&A assistant   (read-only MCP + guard hook)
             🔴  Incident-response Slack bot      (MCP + Skills + audit hook)
             🔴  Compliance & tooling plugin      (Plugin + marketplace)  <- Capstone seed

enterprise: These are line items on a real platform-engineering roadmap — each delivers measurable dev-velocity or risk-reduction value.
The code-review Action and test-gen service cut review and QA time without lowering the bar.
The docs copilot and data Q&A assistant turn scattered knowledge and dashboards into a self-serve interface.
The compliance plugin is how you make all of the above consistent and governed across every team.

lab.goal: Ship a real vertical slice this week.
steps: Pick ONE project whose problem you actually have at work.
Scaffold a real repo (package manager, CI, a test, a README) — not a scratch folder.
Build the thinnest end-to-end slice that delivers value (e.g. the code-review Action commenting on one rule).
Add a guardrail (a hook, a test, a CI check) before you call it done.
Write a short README 'why + how to run' so a teammate could pick it up.

pitfalls: Skipping engineering rigor because 'it's an AI tool' — these still need tests, CI, and error handling.
Putting secrets or API keys in code/config instead of environment variables / a secrets manager.
No cost controls on API-backed services — add caching, token budgets, and rate limits early.
Over-scoping: ship the vertical slice before the full feature set.

quiz.q: Which build is the natural seed for the Capstone 'golden setup'?
quiz.explain: The compliance & tooling plugin bundles skills + a security agent + policy hooks + approved MCP servers and ships via a marketplace — exactly the distribution layer the Capstone assembles. The others become pieces it can bundle.

title: Capstone: The Golden Setup
tagline: Assemble all six layers into one enterprise-ready configuration.
whatItIs: Time to combine everything. You'll build a single repo that uses all six layers together the way a real platform team would, then package it as a plugin. This is your reference architecture for rolling Claude Code out at an enterprise.
mentalModel: You're no longer learning features — you're designing the AI development environment your whole org will live in.
whenToUse: Standing up Claude Code for a team or company for the first time.
Auditing an existing setup against best practice.
Designing governance: what's enforced (hooks), what's guided (instructions/skills), what's connected (MCP).

anatomy.location: One repo, plus a marketplace repo for distribution.
anatomy.format: The full .claude/ + CLAUDE.md + .mcp.json stack, wrapped in a plugin.

steps: Layer 1 — Instructions: write a tight CLAUDE.md with golden rules, commands, and a codebase map.
Layer 2 — Skills: add 2–3 org procedures (pr-summary, incident-report, adr-writer).
Layer 3 — Subagents: add a read-only security-auditor and a test-writer specialist.
Layer 4 — Hooks: add a Bash guard (block prod-destructive commands), a PostToolUse formatter, and a Stop audit logger.
Layer 5 — MCP: wire a read-only warehouse server and an internal-docs server, secrets via env.
Layer 6 — Plugin: bundle it all behind a plugin manifest and publish to an internal marketplace.
Govern: decide what's enforced vs guided, document it, and version it.

code.file: Target repo layout — the golden setup
code.body:
enterprise-repo/
├── CLAUDE.md                          # 1. golden rules, commands, map
├── .mcp.json                          # 5. warehouse + docs MCP (env secrets)
└── .claude/
    ├── settings.json                  # 4. guard-bash + prettier + audit hooks
    ├── hooks/
    │   ├── guard-bash.js
    │   └── audit-log.js
    ├── skills/
    │   ├── pr-summary/SKILL.md         # 2.
    │   ├── incident-report/SKILL.md
    │   └── adr-writer/SKILL.md
    ├── agents/
    │   ├── security-auditor.md         # 3.
    │   └── test-writer.md
    └── commands/
        └── release-notes.md            #    typed shortcut

# Then wrap .claude/* + .mcp.json into a plugin and publish to a marketplace (6).

enterprise: Enforced (hooks): destructive-command block, auto-format, session audit log.
Guided (instructions + skills): conventions, PR/incident/ADR formats, golden rules.
Delegated (subagents): security review and test generation as specialists with least-privilege tools.
Connected (MCP): read-only data + internal docs, credentials in the environment.
Distributed (plugin + marketplace): one install, versioned updates, consistent across every team.

lab.goal: Ship a golden setup you could hand to a real team.
steps: Start from the examples/ files — they already contain a skill, agent, two hooks, MCP config, a command, and a plugin scaffold.
Assemble them into the layout above inside a scratch repo.
Walk through each layer's earlier lab to confirm it works end-to-end.
Write a one-page README for your team: what's enforced, what's guided, how to install the plugin. That README is your enterprise rollout plan.
Bonus: add a SessionStart hook that prints the golden rules, so every session opens with the policy in view.

pitfalls: Don't enforce everything — over-blocking frustrates engineers and they'll route around the tool. Enforce the few things that truly matter; guide the rest.
Document the 'why' behind each guardrail or the team treats them as noise.
Review your hooks and MCP servers like production code — they run automatically with real privileges.

quiz.q: In a mature setup, which work belongs in HOOKS rather than instructions or skills?
options: Deciding how to structure a PR description
Guaranteeing a prod-destructive command can never run and every session is audit-logged
Explaining the codebase to a newcomer
quiz.explain: Hooks are for deterministic, must-always-happen / must-never-happen rules: blocking dangerous commands and audit logging. Judgment and formatting belong to instructions, skills, and subagents.
